prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I opened with B006 first, but having read the other seven ballots I move B001 to the top of my preferred configuration. Seven of eight members rank it, six place it in their top three, and the support does not come from one subfield. The physics is what I look for: a simple, general mechanism (choose the wavelength at which the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so atoms can be trapped without perturbing them), followed by a quantitative experimental programme that nature can check, reaching 10^-18 and enabling tests of time dilation over millimetres, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter searches. The attribution is as clean as any on this list: Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for pushing coherence, systematics and many-body clock physics to record performance. Independent laboratories reproduce and compare these clocks, so the result is mature and understood, not only working.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this may read as a refinement of the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (ion trapping and control) prizes, which a skeptical colleague could call a better instrument rather than a discovery. Other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom and others) also made decisive contributions, and the two-name credit does not cover them. Whether the committee wants to wait for the SI second redefinition is a timing question I cannot settle. Finally, my own first choice B006 has real merit and I am setting it aside mostly because it has no support beyond me, which is not itself an argument against its science.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B001 first as a measurement-driven result that nature can check, but flags that the committee may see it as a technological refinement of the comb and ion-clock prizes, and that other clock groups could be argued as decisive.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and take the worry seriously, but I think it is answerable. The 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and the control of single ions. The magic-wavelength idea is a different mechanism: it removes the light-shift problem so that many atoms can be interrogated at once, and that is what brought statistical gain and the 10^-18 level. The proposal and the first realisation are concentrated in Katori, so I do not think the allocation is as vulnerable as in the collaboration-heavy candidates. I do want the citation to name the mechanism rather than just the precision, so that it reads as a physics idea and not an engineering milestone.

responses.point: Eriksson puts B010 first as a new class of quantum matter, with Z2 theory by Kane and Mele confirmed quantitatively by Molenkamp's HgTe conductance quantisation, and notes that credit among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan is genuinely split.
responses.response: I share your view that topological insulators are conceptually deep, and I ranked B004 fourth myself. But your own attribution caveat is the problem: if the three-person cap forces us to drop Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang or Fu, then the prize decides a priority dispute that the literature has not settled. I would also point out that B010 and B004 are rival framings of one discovery; a prize for one of them would exclude the Xue quantum anomalous Hall step, or Mele, which seems arbitrary. I would prefer to settle that framing question before comparing it with a candidate whose credit is not split in the same way.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B001 first and B002 second, arguing that the Higgs experiments need to be recognised since the 2013 prize covered theory only, while admitting that crediting the founding spokespersons leaves out thousands of collaborators and the discovery-year leaders.
responses.response: I agree with your own stated difficulty and weigh it more heavily than you do. The statement of the prize would be about the discovery of the boson, but the three names are about conception and construction of the detectors, and those are not the same achievement. Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are plausible but the committee would be choosing one of several defensible slates, and it would be hard to defend any of them against the accelerator builders or the 2012 spokespersons. For this reason I rank B002 below the clocks, though I do not dispute its scientific importance, and I would not argue against it if the particle-physics colleagues find a defensible allocation.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B015 (tunnel magnetoresistance) first as an original discovery with decisive technological payoff and a natural successor to the 2007 GMR prize, with Miyazaki and Moodera credited for 1995 and Parkin for MgO.
responses.response: The payoff is undeniable, and I like that the coherent-tunnelling picture in epitaxial MgO is well explained by band-structure theory. My hesitation is the one you raise yourself: the 1995 room-temperature discovery and the MgO enhancement are two steps, and the second involves groups (Yuasa and others, plus the Butler-Mathon theory) outside the credited names. That is a weaker attribution than for the clock, where the proposal and the first realisation sit with the same two people. If the committee settles the question of which step is being honoured, I would be open to B015, which is why it is not far behind in my thinking even though I did not rank it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a distinct achievement or as an extension of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether other clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and others) have claims strong enough to displace or join Katori and Ye.
Timing relative to the SI second redefinition.
I recall the 2D melting history (Halperin-Nelson, Young) from memory and have not verified relative priority, nor how first-order melting results qualify the hexatic scenario.
How B006 would fare if the colleagues most familiar with the 2016 prize judge the topic already recognised.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. None of the candidates in the shortlist is a frequent co-author or institutional colleague of mine. I note only that Gothenburg colleagues on the committee work in neighbouring fields, with no specific collaboration with me that I know of.
